stories.title: The Last Train to Kota
stories.text:
# The Last Train to Kota

The man across from her was eating a mango with a pocket knife and Maya could not stop watching him.

It was 11:47 PM on the last train out of Sudirman and the carriage was nearly empty and the man was peeling the mango in one long unbroken spiral, the way her father used to do, and Maya had not seen anyone do it that way in eleven years.

"You're staring," the man said, without looking up.

"Sorry."

"It's fine."

The train rattled. Outside the window, the city smeared past in long ribbons of neon — green from a pharmacy sign, red from a bridal shop, the cold blue of a 24-hour ATM. Maya pressed her forehead to the glass. In her bag was a letter from a notary. In the letter was a sentence that began *We regret to inform you* and ended with the word *deceased*.

She had read it four times on the platform. She had not cried.

"You want some?" the man said.

He was holding out a slice of mango on the flat of the knife.

"I don't — "

"It's a good one. Sweet."

She took it. The juice ran down her wrist. The man watched her eat it with a kind of patient attention that made her uncomfortable, and then he said, "You look like someone who got bad news."

"My father died."

She had not said it out loud yet. The words sat there on the table between them like something she had spilled.

"Tonight?"

"Three days ago. I just — I just got the letter."

"Were you close?"

"No."

The man nodded. He cut another slice. He did not say *I'm sorry* and Maya was grateful for it because everyone else had said *I'm sorry* and she had wanted to scream at every one of them.

"My father," the man said, "used to peel mangoes like this. Drove my mother crazy. She said use a plate, use a plate, and he never did."

"Mine too."

"Did he teach you?"

"No. He left when I was nine."

The train slowed. Kota Station glowed ahead in the dark like a lantern. Maya realized her hands were shaking and she put them flat on the table and the man pretended not to notice.

"You know what's strange," she said. "I've been angry at him for so long. I had a whole speech. I was going to say it next time I saw him."

"And now you can't."

"And now I can't."

The man wiped his knife on a napkin and folded it closed.

"My stop," he said.

He stood. He looked down at her, and for a second his face did something that was not quite a smile, and he set the rest of the mango on the table in front of her.

"For the rest of the ride," he said.

She watched him walk down the carriage and step onto the platform. She watched the doors close. She watched the train pull away.

Then she picked up the mango and she ate it with her hands, the way her father had taught her once, on a balcony in Bandung when she was eight years old, and she finally — finally — began to cry.

*The juice ran down her wrists like something forgiving her.*

stories.title: What the Doorman Saw
stories.text:
# What the Doorman Saw

Pak Yusuf had been the night doorman at Menara Cipta for nineteen years and he knew, the moment the woman walked into the lobby at 2 AM, that something was going to happen.

She was not a resident. He knew every resident. She was wearing a wedding dress.

Not a costume. A real one — heavy white satin, the hem grey from the street, one shoulder strap slipping. She walked past his desk without looking at him and pressed the elevator button.

"Ma'am."

She did not turn around.

"Ma'am, I need to see your residence card."

"I'm visiting."

"Ma'am, at this hour I have to call up — "

"Apartment 1408. Reza Pratama."

Pak Yusuf knew Pak Reza. Pak Reza was thirty-four, an architect, and he was getting married next Saturday. Pak Yusuf had signed for the wedding invitations himself.

He looked at the woman.

She was very young. Her mascara had run and dried and run again. Her hands were empty — no bag, no phone, no shoes, he realized. She was barefoot on the marble.

"Ma'am," he said gently, "is Pak Reza expecting you?"

"No."

"Are you — are you the bride?"

She laughed. It was a terrible sound.

"No," she said. "That's the problem."

The elevator dinged. The doors opened. She stepped in and turned to face him and for a second Pak Yusuf saw her clearly — saw a girl, twenty-three or twenty-four, the age of his oldest daughter, standing in a borrowed-looking dress with her chin lifted in a way that meant she was trying very hard not to fall apart in front of a stranger.

He should call up. That was the rule.

He did not call up.

"Floor fourteen," he said. "The button sticks. You have to press it twice."

She nodded. The doors closed.

---

He sat at his desk. He did not look at the security monitors. He looked at the photo on the desk — his wife, dead now four years, smiling at a beach in Pangandaran in 1998. He thought about the night he met her. He thought about a letter he had not sent in 1994 and how his whole life had been different because of it, and how he still, sometimes, at 2 AM in an empty lobby, wondered.

Twenty-two minutes passed.

The elevator dinged.

She came out alone. The dress was the same. Her face was different — emptier, somehow, as if something inside her had finally been set down. She walked toward the door.

"Ma'am."

She stopped.

"Do you — do you need a taxi?"

She shook her head.

"It's raining."

"I know."

She looked at him. For the first time, really looked.

"Thank you," she said, "for letting me go up."

"I didn't do anything."

"You did."

She walked out into the rain. The white dress went grey, then darker. He watched her until she turned the corner and was gone.

In the morning, when the day shift came on, Pak Yusuf did not mention her. He never mentioned her. Three months later, Pak Reza moved out of 1408 — alone, no wife, no wedding photos in the boxes — and Pak Yusuf helped him carry a lamp to his car and did not ask, and Pak Reza did not say.

Some nights, when the lobby was empty, Pak Yusuf thought about the unsent letter from 1994. He thought about how a person's whole life could pivot on a button pressed twice.

He thought: *we are all, every one of us, walking around with a wedding dress in our past.*

Then he wiped down his desk and waited for morning.

stories.title: The Locksmith's Daughter
stories.text:
# The Locksmith's Daughter

The call came at 1:13 AM and Sari knew before she answered that it was him.

"Sar."

"Bapak."

"I locked myself out."

She sat up in bed. The streetlight through the curtain made stripes across her blanket. In the next room her husband shifted, mumbled, slept on.

"Bapak. You're a locksmith."

"I know what I am."

"You have — you literally have keys to every — "

"I left them inside."

She closed her eyes.

"Where are you?"

"Home."

"Whose home?"

A pause.

"The old one."

---

She drove across the city in pajama pants and a jacket. The streets were wet and almost empty. She passed a 24-hour warung where a man was sleeping with his head on the counter, a woman on a scooter with three children somehow balanced behind her, a stray dog crossing slowly as if it owned the road.

The old house was in Menteng. Her mother had lived there until she died. Her father had not lived there in eleven years. Sari had not been back in eight.

He was sitting on the front steps in the rain.

"Bapak. *Astaga*. You're soaked."

"It's warm rain."

"Get up."

He got up slowly. He was seventy-one and he moved like a man who had carried tools for fifty years, which he had. She unlocked the gate with the spare key she had never given back. She unlocked the front door. The house exhaled at her — old wood, dust, the ghost of her mother's jasmine soap.

"I haven't been inside," her father said behind her. "Since."

"I know."

"I just wanted to sit on the steps."

"For how long?"

"A few hours."

"Bapak."

"I couldn't sleep."

She turned on the lamp in the hallway. The bulb still worked. Everything still worked. Her mother's sandals were by the door where her mother had left them in 2014 and her father had not, in eleven years, moved them.

She looked at her father.

He was looking at the sandals.

"Bapak," she said, very carefully, "did you actually lock yourself out?"

He did not answer.

He reached into his jacket pocket and took out a key ring. Six keys. He laid it on the small table by the door. His hand was shaking.

"I didn't know how to ask you to come," he said.

Sari sat down on the floor of her mother's hallway. Her father sat down beside her, slowly, his knees creaking. They did not look at each other. They looked at the sandals.

"I miss her," he said.

"I know."

"I don't know what to do with the missing."

"I know, Bapak."

Outside the rain came harder. Her phone buzzed in her pocket — her husband, probably, wondering. She did not answer it. She put her head on her father's shoulder, the way she had not done since she was a child, and she felt him take a breath that shook all the way down.

A locksmith's daughter learns young: every lock has two sides. The thing that keeps people out is the same thing that keeps people in.

She sat with him until the rain stopped. Then she made tea in her mother's kitchen, and they drank it standing up, and at dawn she drove him home — to the new apartment, the small one, the one that was not haunted — and he kissed her forehead at the door and said *terima kasih, sayang* in a voice she had not heard him use in eleven years.

She drove home in the soft early light.

She was crying. She was also, she realized, smiling.

stories.title: Three Voicemails
stories.text:
# Three Voicemails

The first voicemail was an accident.

Dimas was on the bus, on the way home from the hospital, and his thumb hit her name in his contacts and the call connected before he understood what had happened. He held the phone to his ear. Three rings. Then her voice — *Hi, you've reached Lila, leave a message* — bright and clear and exactly the way he remembered it, even though Lila had been dead for four months.

He ended the call.

He sat there. The bus rocked. Outside, Jakarta at 9 PM was the usual — motorbikes weaving like fish, food carts steaming, a billboard with a smiling family selling insurance.

He called her again.

He let it ring through to voicemail. He listened to her voice. He hung up before the beep.

---

The second voicemail he left on purpose.

It was a Tuesday, three weeks later. He was in the apartment they had shared. He had just finished folding the last of her clothes into a box for her sister, and when he closed the box he found that he could not stand up from the floor.

He took out his phone. He called her.

*Hi, you've reached Lila, leave a message.*

*Beep.*

"Hey," he said.

He did not know what came next. He sat on the floor of their bedroom, holding the phone, and he said:

"I packed your sweaters today. The grey one. The one with the hole in the elbow you said you'd fix and never fixed. I almost kept it. I don't know why I didn't."

He waited. He listened to the silence on the line.

"Your sister called. She wants to know if she should take your books. I told her yes. I think you would want her to have them. She always borrowed them anyway and never gave them back, and you used to get so mad, and — "

His voice broke.

"I miss you. I miss you. I miss you."

He ended the call.

He sat on the floor for a long time.

---

The third voicemail was the one that changed things.

It was a Saturday in November. He had been calling her every few days. Sometimes he just listened. Sometimes he talked. He had not told anyone he was doing this. He was aware, in some distant adult part of his mind, that this was probably not what the grief counselor would recommend.

He dialed.

The phone rang.

A voice he did not know answered.

"Hello?"

He could not breathe.

"Hello? Who is this?"

It was a woman. Young. Confused. Real.

"I'm — I'm sorry," Dimas said. "I think I have the wrong number."

"You called Lila?"

He sat down. He had been standing on his balcony. He sat down on the concrete floor.

"You — you have her number?"

"They reassigned it. I just got this number two weeks ago. I'm sorry, I — there have been a lot of calls. Was she — was she someone you knew?"

"My wife."

"Oh."

There was a long silence. The woman — the stranger, the new owner of Lila's number — did not hang up. He could hear her breathing. He could hear, faintly, a child in the background asking for water.

"I'm so sorry," she said.

"It's okay."

"It's not, but — I'm sorry."

He wiped his face.

"Can I ask you something?" she said. "Can I — would it be okay if I changed my voicemail? Because right now it still — I haven't set it up yet, and so it's still her, and I think — I think people are calling and hearing her. I didn't want to change it without — I don't know why I'm asking you."

Dimas looked out at the city. The lights of a thousand windows. Somewhere in one of them, a stranger was holding a phone and asking him for permission to erase the last recording of his wife's voice on earth.

He closed his eyes.

"Yes," he said. "Please. Change it."

"Are you sure?"

"I'm sure."

"Okay."

"Thank you," he said. "Thank you for asking."

He ended the call.

He did not call the number again.

He stood up. He went inside. He took down the photo of Lila from the bookshelf — not to put it away, but to move it to the bedroom, where he would see it every morning, where it belonged.

The city below him kept going.

He made dinner. He ate it. He went to sleep.

In the morning, for the first time in months, he was hungry.

stories.title: The Night Watchman's Coat
stories.text:
# The Night Watchman's Coat

It was raining the night Pak Hendra realized his son was the thief.

He had been the night watchman at the textile warehouse for twenty-two years. The job was simple: walk the perimeter, check the locks, sit in the small booth by the gate, and stay awake until 6 AM. He had never missed a shift. He had never lost a key. He had, in twenty-two years, caught exactly two thieves — both of them teenagers, both of them scared, both of them released with a warning because Pak Hendra remembered being a teenager and being scared.

The third thief he caught was his son.

---

It was 3:14 AM. Pak Hendra was on his second round. The rain was the soft kind, the kind that meant business, and his old knees were telling him about it. He turned the corner by the loading dock and saw a figure climbing down from the truck bay with a roll of fabric over one shoulder.

He raised his flashlight.

The figure froze.

The figure was Adit.

Adit, who was twenty-six. Adit, who lived with his mother on the other side of the city. Adit, whom Pak Hendra had not spoken to in fourteen months because of an argument about money that had ended with both of them saying things that could not be unsaid.

The rain came down harder.

Neither of them moved.

"Pak," Adit said.

Pak Hendra lowered the flashlight.

For a long moment he could not speak. The rain ran off the brim of his cap and into his collar. He thought about the silent alarm under the desk in the booth. He thought about the security cameras — three of them, one on the loading dock, the footage already recorded, already saved to the server in the office. He thought about his pension. He thought about the framed photograph on his wife's nightstand: Adit at six, holding a kite, laughing.

"Put it back," Pak Hendra said.

"Pak — "

"Put it back."

Adit set the roll of fabric down on the wet concrete.

"Back on the truck."

"Pak — "

"*Back on the truck.*"

Adit climbed up. He set the fabric where it had been. He climbed down. He stood in the rain in front of his father with his hands at his sides like a child waiting to be hit.

"How long," Pak Hendra said.

"What?"

"How long have you been doing this."

A pause.

"Six months."

"Here?"

"Other places. This is the first time here."

"Why."

Adit's mouth opened. Closed. Opened.

"Mama is sick again."

The rain kept falling. Pak Hendra felt something in his chest do a thing that was not a heart attack but was close.

"What do you mean again."

"The cancer. It came back. Three months ago."

"She didn't — "

"She didn't want me to tell you."

Pak Hendra and his wife had been divorced for nine years. They were polite at family weddings. They sent each other birthday messages. They had not, in nine years, had a real conversation.

He took off his coat.

It was the warehouse coat — heavy, waterproof, the company logo on the chest. He held it out to his son.

"Put this on."

"Pak — "

"You're wet."

"Pak, the cameras — "

"I know about the cameras. Put it on."

Adit took the coat. He put it on. It was too big for him. He had always been smaller than his father, even as a grown man.

"There's a back gate," Pak Hendra said. "I unlock it at four for the cleaning crew. You're going to walk out at four. You're going to leave the coat in the bushes by the bus stop. You're going to go home. Tomorrow you're going to call me. We're going to talk about your mother."

"The footage — "

"I'll handle the footage."

"Pak, you'll lose your — "

"I said I'll handle it."

Adit was crying. Pak Hendra had not seen his son cry since Adit was eleven years old.

"Go sit in the booth," Pak Hendra said. "Until four. Don't touch anything."

---

At 4 AM Pak Hendra unlocked the back gate. His son walked out into the rain wearing his father's coat. Pak Hendra watched him until he turned the corner.

Then he went to the office. He sat down at the computer. He looked at the security footage from the loading dock — twenty-three minutes of his son, his coat, their conversation in the rain.

He deleted it.

He walked back out into the rain without a coat. He finished his shift. At 6 AM the day man came on and asked him why he was so wet, and Pak Hendra said the rain had caught him on his round, and the day man laughed and said *Pak, you've been doing this twenty-two years, you should know to bring two coats by now.*

Pak Hendra agreed that he should know.

He drove home. He did not sleep. At 9 AM he called his ex-wife. She answered on the second ring.

"Hen?"

"I want to come see you," he said. "Today. Is that okay."

A long silence.

"Yes," she said. "Yes, Hen. Come."

He hung up. He stood in his kitchen in his wet uniform. He thought: *I was a watchman for twenty-two years and I did not see the one thing I was supposed to see.*

Then he changed his clothes. And he went.

stories.title: The Cake at Midnight
stories.text:
# The Cake at Midnight

Indah was buying a birthday cake at midnight for a husband who had left her three weeks ago.

She did not know she was doing this until she was doing it. She had gone to the 24-hour supermarket for milk. She had walked past the bakery counter. She had stopped. She had stood there for eleven minutes, staring at a small chocolate cake with white piped flowers, and the boy behind the counter had finally said, "Ma'am? Did you want that one?"

And she had said yes.

"Anything written on it?"

She almost said *no.*

"Selamat Ulang Tahun, Bayu," she said.

The boy wrote it in blue icing. His hand was steady. He was maybe nineteen, with a very small mustache he was clearly proud of, and he did not ask why a woman was buying a birthday cake at midnight for a man who was not with her. Indah was grateful for this. She paid. She carried the cake out to her car in its small white box, and she sat in the parking lot, and she did not start the engine.

Bayu's birthday was tomorrow.

Bayu had moved out on the third of the month. He had taken his clothes, his books, his guitar, and the framed photograph from their wedding that had hung in the hallway. He had left her the apartment, the cat, and a note that said *I'm sorry. I can't do this anymore. I'll call you.*

He had not called.

She had not called him.

She sat in the parking lot with the cake on the passenger seat. The streetlight made a soft halo through the box's plastic window. She could see the *B* of *Bayu*, blurred by condensation.

She drove.

She did not drive home.

---

His sister's apartment was in Tebet. Indah had been there twice, both times with Bayu, both times for family dinners that had ended in the kind of warm noisy laughter that had made her, both times, briefly believe she had married into the right family.

She parked across the street. She looked up at the third floor. The light was on.

She did not get out of the car.

She took out her phone. She scrolled to his sister's number. She had not deleted it. She had not, she realized, deleted any of them — not his mother, not his cousins, not the WhatsApp group called *Keluarga Besar* that she had been quietly muted in for three weeks.

She typed: *Mbak. I'm downstairs. I have something for Bayu. Is he there?*

She deleted it.

She typed: *Mbak. Sorry to bother you. I bought a cake by accident.*

She deleted it.

She typed: *Mbak.*

She stared at the single word for a long time.

She deleted it.

She put down the phone.

She looked at the cake.

---

She drove home.

The cat met her at the door, complaining. She fed the cat. She put the cake on the kitchen counter. She stood there in her coat looking at it, and at the clock — 12:47 AM, officially Bayu's birthday now, the first one in eight years she would not spend with him — and something in her, very quietly, broke.

Not loudly. Not dramatically. Just — broke. Like a thin plate set down too hard.

She took out a fork.

She sat on the kitchen floor, with her back against the cabinet, and she opened the box.

*Selamat Ulang Tahun, Bayu.*

She ate the *B* first.

She ate slowly. Methodically. The cake was too sweet. The icing flowers were the kind that made your teeth hurt. She did not stop. She ate every letter of his name, and then she ate every letter of *Selamat Ulang Tahun*, and then she ate the white piped flowers, and then she ate the cake.

The cat watched her from the doorway.

When she was done, she put the empty box in the bin. She washed the fork. She drank a glass of water. She sat on the kitchen floor again because she did not have the strength to stand.

She thought: *I have just eaten my husband's birthday.*

She started to laugh.

She could not stop laughing. The cat came over and sat on her foot, concerned, and Indah laughed harder, and then the laughing turned into crying, and then the crying turned back into laughing, and somewhere in the middle of all of it, sitting on the kitchen floor with chocolate on her teeth, she understood — clearly, for the first time, in a way that no friend or therapist or sister had been able to make her understand — that he was not coming back. And that this was not the end of her.

She stood up.

She washed her face.

She brushed her teeth twice.

She went to bed.

In the morning she would block his number. She did not know this yet. She would block it at 9:14 AM, between coffee and the start of her workday, and she would feel, when she did it, the way you feel when you finally take off a shoe that has been hurting you all day.

But that was tomorrow.

For now, she slept. The cat slept on her chest. Outside, the city slept. Somewhere across town, a man she had loved for eight years was turning thirty-four without her, and Indah Kartika, lying in the dark with chocolate still on her breath, was learning the difference between losing someone and being free.

She slept until noon. She had not done that in years. When she woke up, she was hungry.

stories.title: The Boy in 5C
stories.text:
# The Boy in 5C

The boy in 5C had been crying for forty minutes and his mother was not going to make it.

Rina knew this the way she knew most things on a red-eye out of Jakarta: from watching. Twenty-three years as a flight attendant had taught her to read a cabin in three seconds. The mother in 5D was thirty, maybe thirty-one, with the rigid shoulders of a woman trying very hard not to come apart. The boy was four. He was crying in the specific exhausted way of a child who has stopped knowing why he is crying and only knows that he cannot stop.

The man in 5B was making a face.

Rina did not like the face.

She walked down the aisle slowly. The plane was forty minutes into a six-hour flight to Tokyo. The lights were dim. Most of the cabin was asleep or pretending to be.

"Ma'am," she said gently.

The mother looked up.

Up close she was younger than Rina had thought. Twenty-eight, maybe. She had not put on lipstick. Her hair was in a bun that had given up two hours ago. She had a small notebook open on her tray table, full of crossings-out, and Rina recognized — instantly, the way one drowning person recognizes another — the handwriting of someone trying to write a letter she did not want to write.

"I'm so sorry," the mother said. "I'll — I'll get him to stop. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry."

"Ma'am — "

"He's never like this. He's a good boy. We're going to — we're going — "

She could not finish the sentence.

"Where are you going?" Rina said.

"Tokyo."

"For a holiday?"

The mother looked at her. Just looked. And Rina understood.

"My husband is — " the mother said. "He's — there was an accident. We're going to — to bring him — "

The boy, who had been crying with his face buried in her side, lifted his head.

"Mama," he said. "I want Papa."

The mother's face did a thing that Rina had seen before, on this aircraft, on other aircraft, in the small hours of long flights: it closed. Like a door pulled shut against a wind. She put her hand on the boy's head. She could not speak.

"What's your name?" Rina said to the boy.

He did not answer. He pressed his face back into his mother.

"His name is Aksa," the mother whispered.

"Aksa," Rina said. "I'm going to tell you a secret. Are you ready?"

The boy did not move.

"On every airplane," Rina said, "there is one special seat. Just one. It's the seat where the captain lets one passenger sit and help fly the plane. Tonight that seat is empty. Would you like to sit in it?"

The boy lifted his head one centimeter.

"Where?" he said.

"In the back. Near my jump seat. You can watch the lights."

The mother started to say *no, he can't*, and Rina caught her eye and the mother stopped.

"Just for a little while," Rina said. "So your mama can rest."

The mother's eyes filled. She nodded.

---

The jump seat was at the back of the cabin, in the dim space behind the last row, by the galley. Rina strapped Aksa into the seat next to hers. She gave him a plastic cup of warm water. She gave him her flashlight to hold. He held it like a small sword.

"Are you a captain?" he said.

"No. I'm a flight attendant."

"What's a flight attendant?"

"I help people on the plane."

"Oh."

He was quiet for a while. The plane hummed around them. Rina could hear, from the front of the cabin, the silence that meant his mother was finally crying — quietly, into a tissue, the way some women cry when they have been holding it for days.

"My papa," Aksa said.

"Yes."

"Mama said he went to sleep."

Rina looked at him. Four years old. Pajamas under his clothes — she could see the cuffs of dinosaur pajama pants below the hem of his jeans. He had a small bandage on his elbow.

"Is that right?" she said carefully.

"Mama said he went to sleep and we have to go bring him home."

"That sounds right."

He thought about this.

"I don't want him to be asleep."

"I know, sweetheart."

"I want him to wake up."

Rina did not say anything. She did not say *he will,* because that would be a lie. She did not say *I'm sorry,* because she was a stranger and it was not her grief to claim. She sat next to him in the dim humming dark and she let him hold her flashlight.

After a while he leaned against her arm.

After a while he was asleep.

She carried him back to 5C an hour later. His mother was asleep too — the notebook had fallen to the floor, the pen still in her hand. Rina settled the boy into his seat. She covered them both with a blanket. She picked up the notebook.

She could not help reading the top line.

*Aksa, when you are older, I want you to know about your father. I want you to know — *

She closed the notebook. She slid it back onto the tray table.

She stood there for a moment in the dim cabin, watching them sleep. The mother's hand had found the boy's in sleep. They were holding on to each other like people in a small boat.

---

When they landed in Tokyo, the mother thanked her. She did not know how to thank her enough. She kept saying it — *terima kasih, terima kasih, terima kasih* — and Rina kept saying *it's nothing, it's nothing,* and they both knew it was not nothing.

At the door of the aircraft the boy turned around.

"Bu," he said.

"Yes, Aksa."

"Are you going to fly back?"

"Yes."

"Tonight?"

"In a few hours."

He thought about this. Then he held out his small fist. In it was the flashlight she had given him to hold.

"For the next kid," he said.

She took it.

She watched them walk down the jet bridge — a small woman, a smaller boy, going to collect a body in a foreign city at five in the morning.

Then she turned around and she went back into the cabin and she began, with the other crew, to clean up for the next flight. She put the flashlight in her apron pocket. She kept it there for the rest of her career. Twelve years, until she retired. She gave it, on her last flight, to a young flight attendant on her first shift.

"For the next kid," she said.

The young woman did not understand.

Rina did not explain.

Some things you only learn at 35,000 feet, in the dark, holding the hand of a stranger's child.

stories.title: The Rooftop Garden
stories.text:
# The Rooftop Garden

The tomatoes were dying and Pak Surya did not know how to tell his wife.

He had been growing them on the rooftop for six years. Twelve plants. Cherry tomatoes, Roma tomatoes, one heirloom variety that his wife had ordered the seeds for from a catalog in 2019, back when she could still climb the four flights of stairs to see them. The garden was hers. He only watered.

Now the leaves were curling. Black spots. He had looked it up: *Phytophthora infestans*. The same blight that had starved Ireland in 1847. He was a retired engineer. He understood causes. He could not save them.

He sat on the white plastic chair on the rooftop at 11 PM. The city below was a circuit board of lights — orange of streetlamps, white of office towers still working late, the occasional red blink of a plane descending toward Soekarno-Hatta. The rooftop smelled of dying tomato leaves and the jasmine from the planter Bu Ratna had insisted on, even though he had told her jasmine attracted ants.

She had been right about the jasmine. The smell was — she had said — *the smell of being alive in a city that pretends not to be.*

She was downstairs now. Bed 1. Hospice nurse came at 8 AM and 8 PM. She had stopped eating on Tuesday. The doctor had said *days, not weeks,* in the gentle careful voice doctors used when they wanted you to understand without making you understand.

Pak Surya looked at the tomatoes.

He thought: *I cannot let her see them like this.*

---

He drove to the 24-hour supermarket.

It was strange to be out at midnight. He was seventy-three years old. He had not driven at midnight since his daughter's wedding in 2008. The roads were emptier than he remembered. The traffic lights changed for no one. He passed a man pushing a noodle cart, a woman walking a small dog, three teenagers on a single scooter laughing at something on a phone.

In the supermarket, the produce aisle was almost empty. He found the tomatoes. He bought all of them — every Roma, every cherry, every vine-ripened beefsteak. The cashier, a young man with sleepy eyes, stared.

"Pak. You having a party?"

"No."

"That's a lot of tomatoes."

"My wife likes tomatoes."

The young man scanned them. There were forty-seven. The total was 312,000 rupiah. Pak Surya paid in cash.

"Pak," the young man said, as he was bagging them, "is your wife okay?"

Pak Surya looked at him.

The young man flushed.

"Sorry, Pak. It's just — sometimes people come in late and buy strange things, and — sorry. I shouldn't have — "

"She is dying," Pak Surya said.

The word landed in the fluorescent supermarket light like a small bird hitting a window.

"Pak. *Astaga.* I'm so sorry."

"It's alright."

"The tomatoes — "

"They're for her garden. She thinks they're still growing. I want her to see them growing."

The young man's face did something that Pak Surya had been seeing on faces all week and had begun to find unbearable. He looked away.

"Pak. Wait."

The young man went to the back. He came out with a roll of green garden wire, the kind used to tie tomato vines to stakes. He did not scan it. He put it in the bag.

"For tying them on," he said. "So they look real."

"I can pay — "

"Pak. Please."

Pak Surya looked at the young man. He thought: *this boy is somebody's son. Somebody made him. Somebody taught him to do this.*

"Terima kasih," he said.

"Take care, Pak."

---

He spent two hours on the rooftop in the dark, with a flashlight clipped to his shirt pocket, tying supermarket tomatoes onto the dying vines.

It was harder than he had expected. The supermarket tomatoes were heavier than the real ones. The vines could not hold them. He had to use extra wire. He had to clip away the worst of the blackened leaves so the green of the bought tomatoes would show. His knees hurt. His back hurt. At 2 AM he sat down on the white plastic chair to rest, and he started to cry, and once he started he could not stop, and he sat on the rooftop of his apartment building under the orange Jakarta sky and cried in a way he had not cried in fifty-one years of marriage, not even at his father's funeral, not even when his daughter was born.

When he was done, he finished tying the tomatoes.

He went downstairs. He washed his face. He sat by his wife's bed. She was awake — she was awake more at night now than during the day, which the hospice nurse had said was normal — and she looked at him with the soft slow eyes of a woman who was already partly somewhere else.

"Sur."

"Yes, sayang."

"You smell like the rooftop."

"I was checking the plants."

"At three in the morning?"

"I couldn't sleep."

She smiled. Her hand found his.

"How are my tomatoes."

He took a breath. He held her hand. He looked at her — at her face, at her thin shoulders, at the woman who had ordered seeds from a catalog in 2019 because she had wanted to grow something heirloom, something old, something that connected her to other gardens in other countries in other years.

"They're beautiful," he said.

"Are they ripe?"

"Some of them. The cherries especially."

"Will you bring me one tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"In the morning. When the light comes through the window."

"Yes, sayang."

She closed her eyes. Her hand stayed in his.

"Sur."

"Yes."

"Thank you for the garden."

He could not speak.

"All these years," she said. "I know I made you carry the water."

"I didn't mind."

"I know."

She slept.

---

In the morning he carried up a cherry tomato on a small white plate. He had washed it. He had set it on a green leaf from the basil plant, because she liked things to look like they were from a magazine. He brought it to her bed. The light was coming through the window the way she had asked.

She was awake.

She looked at the tomato.

She looked at him.

She smiled — the slow soft smile of a woman who knew exactly what her husband had done in the dark, who had perhaps known the moment he came in smelling of the rooftop, and who had decided, in her last days, to let him have it.

"Beautiful," she said.

She ate half. She gave him the other half.

"Sur," she said.

"Yes."

"Next year. Plant the heirlooms again."

"Yes, sayang."

"Promise."

"I promise."

She died on a Thursday.

In the spring, he planted the heirlooms again. He carried the water himself. They grew. They did not get the blight. He ate the first one standing on the rooftop, with the sun on his face, and he said her name out loud to the empty chair, and he kept going.

stories.title: The Translator
stories.text:
# The Translator

The woman wanted Mira to translate a letter from her dead son.

It was 9:47 PM and the translation office was officially closed. Mira had stayed late to finish a contract — Indonesian to English, a shipping dispute, dull and clean — and the woman had knocked on the glass door anyway. Mira had almost not opened it. Something in the woman's face had made her open it.

"You translate?" the woman said. Her English was careful. She was perhaps sixty. Korean, Mira guessed, by the cut of her coat.

"Yes. From what?"

"Korean. To Indonesian."

"I — I do English to Indonesian. For Korean we have — "

"Please."

Mira looked at her.

The woman was holding an envelope. Her hands were shaking.

"Come in," Mira said.

---

The woman sat across the desk. She did not take off her coat. She placed the envelope between them with both hands, the way one places a small animal one is afraid of dropping.

"My son," she said. "He lived here. In Jakarta. Eleven years. He married Indonesian woman. He died — three months ago. Heart. He was forty-one."

"I'm so sorry."

The woman waved this away — not unkindly, just the way a woman waves away a thing she has heard four hundred times and cannot afford to absorb again.

"His wife. She found this." The woman touched the envelope. "In his desk. After. It is letter to me. He wrote in Korean. But — " she stopped. She started again. "His wife, she does not read Korean. She has been carrying this for three months. She does not want to give to translator she does not know. She want — she want a woman."

"I don't read Korean."

"I know."

Mira waited.

"I will read to you," the woman said. "In Korean. You write down what I say in Indonesian. Then I have — I have copy. For her. So she can read what he wrote about her."

"Ma'am — "

"Please."

"You want me to translate it *out loud*. From your reading."

"Yes."

"Why don't you just — write it for her in Indonesian yourself?"

The woman looked at her.

"My Indonesian is small. And — " her voice broke, just slightly, and she steadied it. "And I cannot. I cannot write the words my son wrote. About her. With my own hand. I cannot."

Mira understood.

She took out a fresh notebook. She uncapped a pen.

"Go slowly," she said. "Sentence by sentence. Tell me in English what each sentence says. I will write it in Indonesian for her."

The woman nodded. She took the letter out of the envelope.

She began.

---

*Mama,* she said.

Mira wrote: *Mama,*

*I am writing this because I am thirty-eight years old and I have not told you that I am happy.*

Mira wrote it.

*I have not told you because for many years I thought happy was a thing you got at the end. After the work. After the money. After the success. I thought I would call you when I had it and I would say, Mama, look, I made it. But I am thirty-eight and I have understood something. I am already there. I have been there for a while.*

*Her name is Sari.*

The woman's voice did not change. She read like a woman reading a grocery list. Mira understood that this was the only way she could read it. Mira wrote in Indonesian, very carefully, every word.

*She laughs at things I do not find funny. She is bad at cooking. She sings in the shower in a language I do not understand. She is kind to the gardener and she is kind to the cat and she is kind to me even on days when I am not kind to myself.*

*I want you to know her, Mama. I know you have not met. I know that is my fault. I know you wanted me to marry a Korean girl. I know you said things to me on the phone in 2017 that I have not forgiven you for, and I know you are still angry that I did not come home for Father's funeral, and I know there is a wall between us that I built with my own hands.*

*I am writing to tell you I am ready to take it down.*

*Come to Jakarta, Mama. Come and meet her. I will pay for the ticket. I will pick you up at the airport. I will take you to our house and she will cook for you (badly) and you will hate the food and love her anyway, the way I do, the way you cannot help loving things that are real.*

*I love you, Mama. I have loved you this whole time. I am sorry I made you wait so long to hear it.*

*Your son,*
*Min-jun*

The woman stopped reading.

The office was very quiet.

Mira had stopped writing on the second-to-last sentence. Her hand would not move.

"Ma'am," she whispered.

The woman was not crying. She was sitting very straight. She folded the letter. She put it back in the envelope. She placed her hand on top of the envelope and pressed down, gently, as if to hold something inside it.

"He never sent it," she said. "He wrote it. He put it in the drawer. He died. Three weeks later. He was going to send it. His wife found it."

"Ma'am — "

"I came to Jakarta yesterday. I have never been to Jakarta. His wife — Sari — she met me at the airport. She does not speak Korean. I do not speak Indonesian. We — we held each other in the airport for ten minutes. We could not say anything. She gave me this letter."

The woman finally — finally — let her face break. She did not make a sound. She just sat there as her face broke, and Mira sat across from her and let her, because there was nothing else to do.

After a long time the woman wiped her face with a tissue from her purse. She took the Indonesian translation from Mira's notebook. Mira tore out the pages. She gave them to her.

"How much," the woman said.

"Ma'am. Please. There's no — "

"How much."

Mira looked at her.

"One hundred thousand rupiah," she said softly.

The woman paid in cash. She stood. She put the translation in her purse with the letter.

At the door she turned around.

"Thank you," she said. "For writing it kind."

"He wrote it kind, ma'am. I just — "

"You wrote it kind too. I could hear. Thank you."

She left.

Mira sat at her desk for a long time. Then she closed her notebook. She turned off the lamp. She locked the office. She walked to her car in the parking garage. The city outside hummed with its usual midnight noise — motorbikes, food carts, the distant call to prayer from a mosque that did not sleep.

She thought of her own mother, in Surabaya, whom she had not called in nine days.

She took out her phone. She called her.

"Sayang? *Astaga,* it's late, are you okay?"

"I'm okay, Ma."

"Why are you calling?"

Mira leaned against her car. She closed her eyes. The city went on around her, alive, indifferent.

"I just wanted," she said, "to tell you that I am happy."

A long silence on the other end.

Then her mother, very quietly, in a voice Mira had not heard her use in a long time, said: "Oh, sayang. Tell me. Tell me everything."

And Mira got into her car, and she sat in the parking garage at 11 PM in Jakarta, and she told her mother everything.

stories.title: The Last Customer
stories.text:
# The Last Customer

The warung was closing forever and Bu Tari was making her last bowl of soto when the man walked in.

It was 10:53 PM. The handwritten sign on the door said *Tutup Selamanya — Terima kasih, semua* — *Closed Forever — Thank you, everyone* — and the chairs were already on the tables, and her son was outside loading the freezer onto a truck. Tomorrow morning the building would be torn down. A coffee chain was coming. They had offered her a good price. Her knees were bad and her son lived in Bandung and she was sixty-eight years old, and she had said yes, finally, after thirty-one years.

The last bowl of soto was for her son. She would eat half. He would eat half. They would eat it standing in the empty kitchen and then they would lock the door for the last time and she would give him the key to keep, because she did not want to keep it.

The man at the door said: "Bu. Are you open?"

She looked up.

He was perhaps fifty. He was in a suit. He was wet — it had been raining off and on for hours — and he was holding a small boy by the hand. The boy was maybe six. The boy was also wet. The boy was holding a very small backpack that had a cartoon dinosaur on it.

"We're closed, Pak. Sorry."

"The sign — "

"We close forever tomorrow. Tonight is the last."

The man's face did something she could not read.

"Bu. Please. I — I know it's late. We've been driving. The boy hasn't eaten."

"There are warungs on Jalan Mampang — "

"Bu."

Something in his voice made her stop.

She looked at him properly. His tie was loose. His suit was expensive and rumpled. His left hand was holding the boy's hand and his right hand was holding — she had not noticed — a folded piece of paper. A court paper. She had seen one before, a long time ago, in 1991, when her own husband had — never mind.

She knew what the paper was.

She looked at the boy. The boy was looking at the floor.

"Sit down," Bu Tari said.

---

She took the chair off table three. She wiped it with her apron. She gestured. The man sat. The boy sat. The boy did not let go of his backpack.

"What do you have, Bu?"

"I have one bowl of soto left."

"One?"

"One. I was going to eat it with my son. We can split. The three of us."

"Bu — no — we couldn't — "

"Pak. Sit. The boy is hungry."

The man closed his mouth.

She went to the kitchen. Her son came in from the truck, sweating.

"Ma. Who's out there?"

"A customer."

"Ma, we're closed."

"I know we're closed."

"Then — "

"Beni. Get two more bowls. We're splitting."

Her son looked at her. He had her father's face. He had her father's patience. He sighed the way her father used to sigh, and he got two more bowls.

---

She brought out three bowls of soto. She had stretched it — more broth, an extra hard-boiled egg cut in halves, the last of the fried shallots scattered on top. She had added a small plate of krupuk because the boy looked like he needed krupuk.

She sat down at the table with them. Her son sat down too.

Four people. One last bowl of soto, divided.

The boy ate. He ate the way a tired hungry child eats — with both hands, with his face close to the bowl, with a kind of total attention that made all three adults at the table go quiet and watch him.

The man ate slowly. He ate like a man who had not been hungry in a long time and had forgotten what to do about it.

"It's good, Bu," the man said. "It's very good."

"Thirty-one years," she said. "Same recipe."

"My mother used to make soto."

"From where?"

"Semarang."

"Ah. Semarang soto is different. More yellow."

"Yes."

"Mine is Jakarta."

"I can taste."

They ate.

The boy finished first. He looked at his father. His father pushed his own bowl toward him. The boy ate that too.

After a while the man said, very quietly, looking at his son: "His mother and I separated today."

Bu Tari nodded. She did not say *I'm sorry.* She had learned, in sixty-eight years, that *I'm sorry* was sometimes the worst thing you could say to a person who was holding themselves together with paperclips.

"Where are you going?" she asked instead.

"My sister's. In Depok. We — I just — I didn't want to drive straight there. I needed to — I don't know what I needed."

"You needed soto."

The man laughed. It was a small surprised laugh, the laugh of a man who had not expected to laugh tonight.

"Yes, Bu. I needed soto."

The boy was almost asleep at the table, his cheek on the formica, his small hand still on the spoon.

"Pak," Bu Tari said. "Listen."

The man looked at her.

"Tomorrow," she said, "this place is gone. Tomorrow there will be a coffee shop here. They will sell coffee for fifty thousand rupiah a cup. They will play music. They will not have soto. You and your boy — you came on the last night. You ate the last bowl. Do you understand what I am telling you?"

"I — "

"You came in," she said. "When the door said closed. You came in anyway. And we fed you."

The man's eyes filled.

"Pak," she said. "Your son will remember this night his whole life. He will not remember the paper in your pocket. He will remember the soto. He will remember that on the worst day, his father took him somewhere warm, and a stranger fed him, and he was not alone. Do you understand?"

The man could not speak.

"So tomorrow," she said, "when you drive to your sister's. When you start the new life. You remember: you got in. The door was closed and you got in anyway. That is — Pak — that is the whole thing."

She reached across the table and put her hand on the boy's small hand on the spoon.

"How much," the man whispered.

"No money."

"Bu, please — "

"No money. Last bowl. My gift."

"I — "

"Pak. Take your boy. Drive safe. Go."

---

She walked them to the door. The rain had stopped. The street smelled of wet asphalt and the night-blooming jasmine from the empty lot next door, the lot where, tomorrow, there would be a bulldozer.

The man turned at the door. He held out his hand. She took it. He did not shake it. He just held it for a moment, and then he let go.

"Bu," he said.

"Yes."

"What's your name."

"Tari."

"Bu Tari. Thank you. I will not forget."

"Don't forget. Tell him when he's older."

"I will."

She watched them walk to their car. The boy was almost asleep on his feet. The man picked him up and carried him. The small backpack with the dinosaur swung against the man's back as he walked. He buckled the boy into the back seat. He stood there for a moment with his hand on the car door, and then he got in, and he drove away.

Bu Tari closed the door of her warung for the last time.

She locked it.

She gave the key to her son.

"Ma," her son said. "Why'd you do that. We could have — "

"Beni," she said. "Listen. In thirty-one years of this warung. The last person I fed was a man on the worst day of his life. Do you understand what kind of luck that is? Do you understand what we just did?"

Her son looked at her for a long time.

Then he put his arm around her shoulders, and they walked to the truck together, and they drove home in the warm wet Jakarta night, and behind them, in the empty warung, the smell of soto stayed in the walls until morning, when the bulldozer came.
